title: C# .NET and Oracle Backend Quick Guide
description: Find the key commands, model rules, SQL patterns and reply codes for the Reading List API. Short notes tell you where each piece runs and which mistakes to check.

entries.name: Request and reply
entries.summary: A request asks the API to do one job. A reply has a status code and may contain data. The browser talks to the API; the API talks to Oracle.
notes: GET reads data. POST adds data. PUT changes a known book. DELETE removes a known book.
The site where you read this course is a frontend. You run the teaching API separately.

entries.name: The .NET SDK
entries.summary: The SDK is the tool kit used to create, build and run C# projects. This sample targets .NET 10 and uses Oracle.ManagedDataAccess.Core version 23.26.400.
notes: Run restore and build from the ReadingListApi folder.
A successful build checks code. It does not prove the database is ready.

entries.name: Oracle connection setting
entries.summary: A connection string tells the API which account and Oracle service to use. Keep it in server-side development settings. The browser does not need this value.
notes: Run from the extracted sample root. The helper asks for the local reading_app password with hidden typing. Use the README environment steps for another database address.
The sample project has a UserSecretsId. User secrets stay outside the project, but are not an encrypted password vault.
The environment-variable form of the key is ConnectionStrings__Oracle.

entries.name: Book table shape
entries.summary: Each row is one book. id is a unique numeric label, title is required text, and is_read is 0 or 1. Oracle creates the identity id.
notes: Title allows at most 120 characters in the table.
0 means unread. 1 means read.
Do not assume ids start at 1 or have no gaps.

entries.name: Request model rules
entries.summary: A request model describes the JSON input. Required and StringLength check the title. [ApiController] returns 400 for model validation errors.
notes: Import System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations.
A valid request still needs database work before it becomes a saved book.
The API maps C# bool true/false to the table's 1/0 values.

entries.name: Open and release a connection
entries.summary: OracleConnection is the link used for one piece of database work. Open it before a command runs and release it with using when the work ends.

example.code:
using var connection = new OracleConnection(connectionString);
await connection.OpenAsync();

notes: Import Oracle.ManagedDataAccess.Client and get the setting from the API configuration.
Do not share one open connection across all requests.
The sample's /health endpoint checks the API process, not Oracle.

entries.name: Controller route attributes
entries.summary: A controller route gives actions a shared address. HttpGet, HttpPost, HttpPut and HttpDelete pick the request method and may add an id part.
notes: Program.cs needs AddControllers before Build and MapControllers after Build.
Use the complete controller from the sample when running the app; this short shape only shows its route attributes.

entries.name: Read rows with SELECT
entries.summary: SELECT chooses columns. ExecuteReaderAsync gives a reader that moves through matching rows. ReadAsync returning false means there is no next row.
entries.syntax: SELECT id, title, is_read FROM reading_list_books
notes: The API binds a positive long id to the named :id parameter.
GetInt64(0) reads id, GetString(1) reads title, and GetInt32(2) reads the 0/1 flag.
GET list returns 200 with an array. GET one absent book returns 404.

entries.name: Reply after adding a book
entries.summary: POST saves a new book. A successful reply uses 201 and includes the saved id. Location tells the reader where that new book can be read.
notes: The request supplies title and isRead. Oracle supplies id.
Use the returned id in later requests.
A whitespace-only or overlong title gets 400 instead of creating a row.

entries.name: Change or remove one id
entries.summary: Use a WHERE id = :id rule so a write targets one row. ExecuteNonQueryAsync returns the number of changed rows for this UPDATE or DELETE.
notes: Bind every placeholder before running the command.
This sample returns 204 after a successful PUT or DELETE, and 404 when no row has that id.
A nonpositive id gets 400. Omitting WHERE could affect the whole table.

entries.name: Parameters and transactions
entries.summary: A parameter keeps a value separate from SQL instructions. BindByName matches placeholder names. A transaction groups writes so Commit saves them together and Rollback undoes them.
notes: Never join a title or id into SQL text from a request.
Start a transaction on the open connection before the writes it should cover.
Rollback cancels that transaction's row changes. Identity numbers can still have gaps.

entries.name: Useful status checks
entries.summary: Test saved data and mistakes. A status code is a short label for the result. Check the body too, so a 200 reply does not hide a wrong title.
notes: The example id 0 should receive 400 because ids must be positive.
Create a fresh test book; use its returned id for GET, PUT and DELETE.
After deleting your test book, GET for that same id should receive 404.

entries.name: Origin and CORS
entries.summary: An origin is the scheme, host and port of a web page. CORS tells a browser whether this page may read a reply from a different origin.
notes: The sample allows http://localhost:5500 only when Development:CorsEnabled is true in Development.
Changing the host to 127.0.0.1 or choosing another port changes the origin.
CORS does not log people in or stop a non-browser program from sending requests.

entries.name: Finish a local working copy
entries.summary: Build the sample, run it locally, then test a complete book flow and invalid inputs. Check that your shared files contain no real passwords.
entries.syntax: build → run → create → read → change → delete → check errors
notes: Build success and /health success do not replace a test that writes to and reads from Oracle.
Use only practice book data while learning.
A real shared service needs access rules, HTTPS, suitable error handling, backups and more tests.
